en: The Treatise on the Sun of Wisdom that Illuminates the Middle and the Extremes,
Volume One, composed by the Bhikṣu Huizhao of Dayun Monastery in Zizhou.
The Great Sage Hero, endowed with the ten powers and five eyes, sought the Dharma for the sake of sentient beings throughout boundless eons.
The eighty-four thousand treasuries of wondrous jewels all accord with the true and supreme other shore;
according to the capacities of beings, they are explained and revealed so that each may discern them. Therefore, the Benevolent One is titled the Dharma King.
When the Buddha-sun temporarily hides behind the mountain of Nirvana, the orthodox teaching follows in its concealment and the eye of wisdom perishes.
The assembly of the ten stages, the three levels of worthiness, and all the noble ones—out of compassion for sentient beings and to protect the Dharma, they expounded this profound sutra.
Yet in this final age, life, mindfulness, wisdom, and practice have become feeble;

most follow their own emotions and are deluded regarding the holy intent, interpreting the orthodox teaching according to their own views. Thus, being deluded themselves, they delude others and obstruct the flow of the Dharma.

Now, having selected from the sūtras and śāstras and harmonized these various texts, I have composed this work to provide a comprehensive understanding of the Dharma for the salvation of living beings and to ensure correct realization;
therefore, I prostrate and take refuge in the Triple Gem. I pray that, out of compassion, you will grant your protection;
for the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*) is without discrepancy.
The sūtras and śāstras establish the doctrine of equality;
yet in conventional truth, there are differences.
Among the various noble ones, there are discourses on the fourfold and the oneness.
Following the divisions of the stars of phenomenal wisdom and principle,
one returns to the nature where both mind and speech are utterly transcended;
whether true or conventional.
Alternately real and alternately provisional,
they are measured according to the needs of beings to manifest causes that accord with their capacities and lead toward the fruit;
though the principle is one, [the manifestations differ].
Since capacities are indeed manifold,
the twelve profound portals further distinguish between common and specific aspects;
the deep principles of the Tripiṭaka are explained through either general or analytical classifications.
Some maintain that the "thusness" (tathatā) acts as the cause of arising,
asserting that the essence of mind is the seed of all phenomena;
they cling to this single principle with delusion, refusing to allow for any differentiation.
There are differing difficulties to reconcile;
these are immediately identified as being of the Lesser Vehicle or expedient means,
without realizing that the Tathāgata possesses the power of the various faculties and natures.
Sentient beings possess various dispositions (*dhātu*) and so forth;
some are biased and fixated on specific expressions, causing them all to be inconsistent.
When there is a contradiction, they simply say it is "conforming to convention" or "conforming to the person."
Not knowing that the Blessed One possesses the intention of sameness of essence (*samatā-sarvatraga-abhiprāya*),
they rely on [the teaching of] suchness, indeterminacy, and so forth;
for this reason, the śrāvakas were questioned.
Because he failed to recognize the differences in spiritual capacities,
the Bodhisattva rebuked him;
this was due to his failure to rely on the single principle.
If it is said that True Suchness and Buddha-nature are one,
such that all equally attain Buddhahood without distinction in their spiritual lineage;
In that case, the analogy of the four loads and three grasses would not hold.
If one were to say that icchantikas and those of the two vehicles will both never become Buddhas,
then their spiritual lineages (gotra) would each be singular.
Thus, the analogies of the three vehicles and the two cities would not be established.
Therefore, according to principle, the existence or non-existence [of the potential] depends upon the lineage (*gotra*) within the realm of sentient beings.
Throughout all consciousness,
there are distinctions based on objective referents; thus,
consciousness may exist or not exist.
Those with the nature [of Buddhahood] further differ in being determinate or indeterminate;
those without the nature further differ in being temporary or ultimate.
For this reason, it is said that there are many categories of śrāvakas.
The icchantikas further manifest through repeated submergence;
by means of this, they may attain the fruits of the stages in numbers such as one, two, three, five, or more,
or they may distinguish between the ordinary and the sage, the provisional and the real.
Some say that all possess Buddha-nature and shall all become Buddhas;
others say there are those without the seed-nature and thus not all shall become Buddhas.
Yet, since the causes for Buddhahood differ—whether conditioned or unconditioned—[the results must likewise differ].
The fruit of Buddhahood also possesses both permanent and impermanent aspects.
It is designated as "permanently abiding" based on three meanings,
and it is established with the name "unconditioned" (asaṃskṛta) according to what exists or does not exist therein.
There are some who are confused about this wondrous principle,
claiming that the three Buddhas are collectively quiescent and seeing only the teaching of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
Although one may not know that the four wisdoms are without arising or ceasing,
they are all the Honored One of Right and Universal Knowledge (Samyaksaṃbuddha) based upon the four secrets.
The four kinds of intentions,
whether directed toward oneself or others,
and the twelvefold division of the teachings.
The Buddha himself has harmonized and integrated these teachings,
which are scattered throughout various sutras;
generally speaking, they are difficult to investigate exhaustively.
The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra-vyākhyā* by Maitreya Bodhisattva states:
"In principle, there is nothing not investigated;
in phenomena, there is nothing not exhausted."
There is no passage that is not explained;
there is no meaning that is not elucidated; there is no misconception that is not demolished;
and there is no doubt that is not dispelled.
There are no practices not cultivated;
there are no fruits not realized.
This is precisely what it means to be a bodhisattva.
They cause [beings] to attain skillfulness regarding the objects, practices, and fruits of all vehicles,
and to diligently cultivate the great conduct.
Having realized great enlightenment,
he constantly and unerringly teaches for the sake of sentient beings.
It also serves for those of other vehicles,
enabling them to rely on their own teachings to cultivate their respective practices and attain their own fruits of realization.
Masters such as Asaṅga have provided alternative interpretations of one section.

Alternatively, it may comprehensively clarify the great tendencies [of the teachings], wherein both doctrine and principle are mutually radiant and clear, with the fundamental and the derivative alternating in their brilliance.
Yet sentient beings are mired in obscurity regarding the profound intent;
they seek to fill a small pond with the waters of the great ocean, while the jewel within their own hearts remains shrouded by the garment of their delusions.
To take foul food and cast it into a precious vessel;
to place a string of cities alongside the eyes of a common fish, with no distinction made between plants and trees;
to mix poison with *tīrtha* (clarified butter), where the fragrance of incense and the stench of rotten herbs cannot be distinguished.
Relying on the glow of fireflies to point toward the sun and moon;
daring to scale a precious sword while brandishing a dull lead blade;
thus, the Tāla tree ultimately determines what comes first and last.
Dharma generally distinguishes between the Exoteric and Esoteric;
yet if they mutually inspire one another,
then the essential meaning is contained within the text.
To follow [the literal] and hold it to be the truth is to have words that deviate from reason and principles that fail;
though I am not clever, [I must speak thus].
I have once measured the surging waves of the ocean of Dharma;
yet, mindful of the subtle and profound ways that delude sentient beings, my doubts linger like one facing a perilous precipice, longing for the guidance of the South.
Having encountered these lofty discourses,
I have taken up the pen as a forerunner to gather the subtle and profound essence of the Tripiṭaka.
He expounds the profound essence of the five vehicles,
revealing their hidden subtleties so as to accord with the great path.
This brief exposition in three chapters is intended to awaken those who have not yet attained realization;
though the prose lacks literary elegance, its purpose is clear.
The principle is indeed worthy of contemplation; I hope that those with profound discernment will examine its significance in detail.

Refuting [Fixed Views on] Conditions and the True Buddha-nature 1. Refuting Fixed Views on Time and Causality (Part One) Regarding this, some say:
Within the sūtras and śāstras, there are instances where the names are identical but the meanings differ.
For example, the teaching of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*) in the *Saṃdhinirmocana* and other texts differs from the teaching of the One Vehicle in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* and other texts.
Although these share the same name,
in the *Saṃdhinirmocana*, three are preserved while one is clarified;
in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, two are sublated while one is clarified.
Yet their meanings differ. Why is this?
Because the *Saṃdhinirmocana* maintains [the existence of] two types of cessation (*nirodha*).
It is said that those of the two vehicles with fixed natures do not sit at the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*).
The verse states:
"Therefore, within this [teaching], one vehicle is established."
The nature of non-sentient beings is without distinction;
this exists as three yet is one.
The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* and other texts state:
Whether they be śrāvakas or bodhisattvas,
having heard the Dharma taught by me,
even if it be but a single verse.
All shall undoubtedly attain Buddhahood.
This alone is the one true reality;
the other two are not real.
Abandoning the sheep and deer [drawn by the carts] and extinguishing the conjured city;
shattering the two [vehicles] and extinguishing them to return to the place of treasure—
therefore, the meanings differ.
This explanation is unreasonable.
Why is this so? Because there is no difference in the names or meanings of the various teachings on the One Vehicle (ekayāna).
The profound and esoteric *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* briefly enumerates their commonalities;
for instance, the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*) of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* is equivalent to that of the *Saṃdhinirmocana*.
Furthermore, since the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* cites the prophecy concerning Śāriputra from within the assembly of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, [the two are consistent].
Among these ten points,
how can it be said that before the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, a distinct One Vehicle was taught? Furthermore,
why does the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* explain only the One Vehicle prior to that [sūtra] and not the One Vehicle of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*?
Since they are explained in the same way,
it is clear that there is no distinction between them.
Furthermore, those of fixed nature (niyata-gotra) do not manifest [the path], yet it is said that they can attain Buddhahood.
In the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*,
Mahāmati asks the Buddha, who replies:
"Those who formerly made the vow for bodhicitta are not fixed [in their destiny]," and so forth.
In the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra-śāstra*,
it is stated that because the faculties of those who are determined have not yet matured,
the Bodhisattva grants them a prediction of enlightenment in order to cause them to resolve their minds [upon awakening].
Since the verbal expression was already general,
he further recounted past events;
having thus explained the destruction of the two types of cessation.
The One Vehicle is for the sake of clear manifestation;
that is to say, one must definitively state that both vehicles will all become Buddhas.
Why, then, exclude the definitive?
Furthermore, the third analogy is for those who seek exclusively the Mahāyāna;
it means that apart from the Mahāyāna, there are no separate two vehicles (Hīnayāna).
In order to make known the differences among the various vehicles (*yāna*),
the metaphor of rain is taught. Therefore,
those of the lineage who are intent on profound secrecy and tranquility do not sit upon the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*).
The Lotus Sūtra was taught solely for those who have regressed from the bodhicitta and for transformed śrāvakas;
throughout the three turnings, it expounds the One Vehicle,
and all the śrāvakas to whom it is granted are exclusively these two types.
The Sūtras and Śāstras are in agreement:
there is, in total, no one who attains quiescence;
this is clearly evident within the texts themselves.
Therefore, those of the indeterminate lineage who possess the profound and secret [nature] are all capable of proceeding toward perfect enlightenment.
As the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* says:
"I desire to reveal to sentient beings the Buddha’s knowledge and vision."
The commentary explains the meaning of "sameness" as follows:
"Sameness" refers to the equality of the dharma-body (dharmakāya) of the three vehicles.
Regarding the equality of the dharma-body of the three vehicles:
Because the Buddha-nature and the Dharma-body are without distinction;
this is identical to the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra*’s reliance on the three non-natures and the ultimate non-nature,
and likewise corresponds to the *Liang* commentary’s statement that the One Vehicle is taught based on the equality of phenomena and suchness.
In the Lotus Sutra,
the four great śrāvakas each speak of their own parables:
they were originally lowly laborers hired to remove filth.
During the interim, he had no desire to take the entrusted wealth for himself;
only after gathering the assembly and announcing [the truth] did realization arise.
This is identical to the third-period teaching of the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra*.
Furthermore, the fact that they do not explain the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*) of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* is fully evident from the *Śāstrasaṃgraha* texts of both the Liang and Tang dynasties,
which include categories of phenomena such as the selflessness of all dharmas (*dharmanairātmya*).
Therefore, the discourse on identity and difference is merely a false conceptual construction.
Furthermore, it is said:
"There may be cases where names differ while the substance is identical."
The essence of nirvāṇa and buddha-nature is precisely suchness (*tathatā*).
In the *Buddhadhātu-śāstra*, it is termed "that which is to be attained.
Since it is already admitted that this principle of nature (*li-xing*) pervades all sentient beings.
To claim that one who lacks faith will necessarily become a Buddha is also unreasonable;
for although the causes and conditions for such attainment may exist, [faith is nonetheless required].
However, since it is admitted that Bodhisattvas of Great Compassion possess the causes consisting of applied effort (*prayoga-hetu*),
they do not constantly become Buddhas because the realm of sentient beings is inexhaustible;
why then would this invalidate the fact that sentient beings, though possessing the causes for attainment, [do not attain it]?
Because there is no cause consisting of preparatory effort, he would eternally fail to become a Buddha.
If one were to say, "I accept that he is an agent," this would contradict the sūtras.
Regarding the presence or absence of preparatory application (*prayoga*),
this will be explained in detail later in the main section.
One interpretation states:
Because there are conditions that are correct,
the fruits have near and far [distances].
These conditions are precisely the associated wholesome states and so forth.
This refers precisely to the eight consciousnesses and the nature of the Tathāgatagarbha;
these eight consciousnesses are simultaneously perfected.
True Suchness (tathatā) is omnipresent;
even if the causal conditions are lacking,
it will certainly manifest through cultivation.
"To disbelieve the true cause—
is this not delusion? Their adherence to the contrary is not so."
Furthermore, regarding the claim that True Suchness (tathatā) is the direct cause (hetu):
is it designated as "direct" in view of its producing a fruit,
or is it designated as "direct" based on its being the locus of both delusion and awakening?
That which can produce a fruit is called the "direct cause" (*hetu*).
That which is universally contrary to the sūtras and treatises and is not a cause of production is [the eternal]. *Bodhisattvabhūmi*, Chapter Four.
The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicle 38;
the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*, fascicle 30:
"Because of the four conditions, there is no [intrinsic nature]."
To assert that there is a permanent dharma, and to claim that this permanent dharma serves as a causal condition,
completely contradicts the meaning of "seeds" (*bīja*) as presented in the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*.
If it is claimed that those [conditions] are both objective conditions (*ālambana-pratyaya*) and contributory causes (*hetu-pratyaya*), yet do not directly produce the fruit,
this contradicts all the sūtras and śāstras.
This would constitute a great error.
Furthermore, do you not allow that the body of the Buddha is endowed with the five aggregates?
If it is endowed with the five aggregates, [then...]
Since the cause itself is not even subsumed within the aggregates,
how could it be the cause of the aggregates?
Furthermore, the *Buddhadhātu-śāstra* does not allow that reality can truly give rise to existence.
Therefore, although the eight consciousnesses constitute the direct cause,
this is not said with reference to the consciousnesses as they manifest from time immemorial.
As the Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra states:
Because it is fully endowed with the perfuming of untainted dharmas,
it is called the "non-empty Tathāgatagarbha.
If one takes the consciousness of beginningless active manifestation as the direct cause of Buddhahood, [it would be empty].
Since it is the very cause of Buddhahood, untainted (anāsrava), and constantly manifesting,
how could there be ordinary beings?
If you say it is tainted (sāsrava), [then...]
How, then, can this be considered the direct cause?
This contradicts the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*, which states that poison becomes nectar.
Furthermore, are the mind and mental factors not indeed the direct cause of the Reward Buddha (*vipākabuddha*)?

If it were not for the fact that the four wisdom-minds (catur-jñāna-citta-varga) as described in the *Vyūharāja-śāstra*, the *Saṃgrahaṇī-śāstra*, and other texts are designated as the Reward Body (saṃbhoga-kāya),
one would have to accept them as the Reward Buddha (saṃbhoga-buddha).
If you ask why it is so extreme to claim that things such as "concordant virtues" serve as the causal condition (*pratyaya-hetu*),
yet [you maintain that] True Suchness (*tathatā*) is the direct cause (*hetu-hetu*) of the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*).
It is not other than two:
namely, arising and ceasing.
Thus, true suchness is viewed in relation to the dharma-body.
It is not subsumed under the cause of production;
how, then, can it be called the "direct cause"?
One may only concede that the states of cause and effect are distinct.
It is called the *tathāgatagarbha* in its causal state, and the *dharmakāya* in its resultant state;
it is like the suchness of non-arising.
Furthermore, it does not manifest itself;
since it is neither produced nor extinguished,
one does not know by what principle it could serve as the direct cause.
Because the essence does not undergo change throughout the two stages,
we provisionally distinguish between cause and effect, conditions and the primary, and the real and the delusive. [This is explained] below in the section on the "Correct Cause of the Three Bodies."
This is explained in detail within the Manifestation of the Middle Way (*Madhyāntavibhāga*).
According to one interpretation, those who have long practiced as Bodhisattvas achieve the capacity for upholding [the teachings].
One who abides in the nature of their own vehicle will necessarily attain Buddhahood;
until this stage is reached,
it is said that one does not become a Buddha.
There are those who, being deluded, are incapable of the lineage of their own vehicle as bodhisattvas;
because they are unable to sustain the initial arousal of the mind of enlightenment,
it is said that they lack the spiritual lineage (*agotra*).
To claim, therefore, that those of the "lineage-less" (agotra) nature can never become Buddhas is also unreasonable. Why is this so?
The *Bodhisattvabhūmi-sūtra* states:
"Because of the initial arousal of the mind of awakening, one will certainly and inevitably attain unexcelled perfect enlightenment.
The *Bodhisattvabhūmiviniścaya-saṃgrahaṇī* states:
What is meant by "upholding"?
It refers to the Bodhisattva’s own spiritual lineage and their initial generation of the mind of enlightenment.
And all factors conducive to enlightenment (bodhipakṣadharma).
This is called "upholding. Why is this so?

Because a bodhisattva who relies on the spiritual lineage (gotra) is necessarily capable of attaining unexcelled enlightenment (anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi), the spiritual lineage is called "the definitive support. It continues thus:
[as stated in the text].
Therefore, the initial arousal of the mind is called the Bodhisattva’s practice of maintaining skillful means.
By relying on this practice of skillful means, the Bodhisattva fulfills unexcelled bodhi.
Since it has been stated, "Therefore, the initial arousal of the mind is called the Bodhisattva’s practice of maintaining skillful means," [it follows that this is the case].
Since one fulfills bodhi by relying on the practice of skillful means,
how can it be said that it is only through long-term cultivation that one is called "upholding" [the lineage] or that one possesses its nature?
Furthermore, the *Bodhisattvabhūmi-sūtra* states:
If one lacks the bodhisattva-nature,
then even if they resolve their mind toward awakening and diligently cultivate vigor,
they will ultimately be unable to attain anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Therefore, one should know that it is not because of the arousal of the thought of enlightenment and the diligent cultivation of vigor that there is the bodhisattva-nature; rather,
when one has practiced for a long time until reaching the stage of being capable of upholding [the path], it is then called having the lineage (gotra).
How is it that the Sūtra states that there is no bodhisattva nature for those who do not give rise to the mind [of awakening]?
Furthermore, the *Bodhisattvabhūmi-śāstra* states:
"Those who lack the lineage have no lineage."
Even if one has resolved to attain awakening and diligently cultivates vigor,
one will certainly not reach the ultimate state of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
Therefore, you should know this.
Although one has not yet resolved to attain enlightenment nor practiced the skillful means,

one is still said to possess the "possession of the lineage" (gotra-dhāraṇa). Since it is stated that even without having resolved to attain enlightenment, one is called the "possession of the lineage," [it follows that this is so].
Why trouble oneself with the arbitrary distinction between "initial" and "subsequent"?
Some say this is because they have seen the texts concerning the five natures (*pañca-gotra*) of the Hīnayāna.
This refers to the inherent distinctions among the vehicles of the Three Vehicles,
or to those who lack the cause for nirvāṇa and are ultimately devoid of nature.
This refers to the Adantika, who lack the seeds of the Dharma-nature;
they do not know that all things are ultimately without intrinsic nature, and thus they lack the cause for generating the resolve for enlightenment.
At a later time, there will still be the distinctions of the five vehicles;
all spiritual lineages (gotra) are newly perfumed and arise [through practice].
The text of the Śrāvaka-bhūmi is not a definitive proof [to the contrary].
This statement is entirely incorrect.
Why? Because the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* was composed by Maitreya Bodhisattva.
To say that this is not a definitive proof because it was proclaimed by Śrīmālā, Bhadrapāla, and Śākyamuni, the World-Honored One,
and thus should be considered a Hīnayāna teaching— [is incorrect].
Such is their ferocity and perversity;
who would dare to speak with them?
Yet they claim that there is ultimately no intrinsic nature and no cause for the arousal of the bodhicitta.
Later, it will exist again.
Now I ask him: does the subsequent arising of the thought of enlightenment originate from a seed?
If it arises without a cause—
meaning that the mind naturally arises where there was originally no cause—
one is not a son of the Śākya.
Therefore, the first fascicle of the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* in four fascicles states:
"Mahāmati, if it is further said that there is no seed,
there are three kinds of consciousness."
If things were produced through the combination of three conditions,
then tortoises should grow hair and sand should yield oil.
Your own tenet would then be undermined,
contradicting the definitive meaning.
Furthermore, if you do not admit that the five vehicles possess distinct natures established by the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) from beginningless time, [your position fails].
However, because they are all of the same suchness (tathatā), they shall all attain Buddhahood.
As for those who hold that the five natures (pañca-gotra) are newly perfumed and not inherently existent:
How is it that the World-Honored One causes those of the five natures to be perfumed?
Why does he not merely teach the Mahāyāna so that they may equally perfume the Buddha-seed?
As the Vimalakīrti Sūtra says:
"He himself has no wound;
do not injure him," and so forth.
How could the Great Master, the Tamer of Men, not know that there exists the cause for what ought rightly to be attained?
It is because they disparage them by means of the Hīnayāna.
If one were to say that this is due to differences in their spiritual capacities (indriya),
then it follows that the five natures (pañca-gotra) are inherently existent.
Is it not merely through new cultivation?
Furthermore, the *Bodhisattvabhūmi Sūtra* states:
"It is not by means of generating the resolve [for awakening] and diligently practicing with vigor [that one attains it]."
Because there is the nature of a bodhisattva, we know that all five natures are inherently present from the beginning.
From these inherently present seeds, they arise repeatedly in manifestation; when these are perfumed to form seeds, this is called the "cultivated nature" (*bhāvanā-dhātu*).
Furthermore, the *Śīla-sūtra* and other texts explain the distinct causes for liberation, stating:
"There is the śrāvaka-nature;
one attains parinirvāṇa by means of the Śrāvaka-yāna," and so forth.
Thus, one knows that the distinction between spiritual lineages does not arise from new perfuming.
If it were only through new perfuming that they first came to exist,
then one would have to say that the śrāvaka lineage did not previously exist.
Since it does not state that one causes the nature of the Śrāvaka vehicle to arise and then relies upon the Śrāvaka vehicle and so forth,
it is clear that this is neither something newly produced nor a minor teaching.
Therefore, it is only the principle of "newly arising" that contradicts the scriptural teachings;
however, when the *Mahāsaṃnipāta* and other sutras speak of the existence of perfuming (*vāsanā*),
they do so with reference to the seeds of cultivation (*śikṣā-bīja*).
It is not the nature-seed-lineage (prakṛti-gotra).
If one speaks of the nature-seed-lineage,
it is the principle of True Suchness (tathatā).
That which is not of the nature of practice will be demonstrated below;
this briefly dispels four delusions.
The remaining cases may be inferred by analogy.
2. Regarding the two occasions of destroying the established teaching: there is one interpretation that the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra* was taught earlier.
It is taught that after his parinirvāṇa,
on the twenty-first day, the Wheel of the Four Noble Truths was established as a distinct period of teaching.
After forty years, this is the greatest wheel of Dharma;
why not permit the establishment of a further period for teaching?
Furthermore, the Mahāyāna differs from the Hīnayāna.
Later, when establishing the teachings of the Mahāyāna,
the One Vehicle (ekayāna) was distinguished from the Three Vehicles;
subsequently, the One Vehicle was further expounded.
For what reason is it not permitted to establish the periods of the teachings separately?
Therefore, based on the *Saṃdhinirmocana*,
the first three [turnings] are established.
To claim that the One Vehicle of the Lotus Sūtra constitutes the fourth period and the Buddha-nature of the Nirvāṇa Sūtra constitutes the fifth period is likewise incorrect.
There are many faults. For instance,
regarding the turning of the Four Noble Truths,
at the time when the teaching was subsequently established:
These were spoken by the Buddha, the World-Honored One.
Regarding the One Vehicle as the fourth and the Buddha-nature as the fifth,
the sutra does not determine who spoke them.
If one were to establish five periods of teaching based on their distinct meanings,
every scripture would have its own specific intended meaning.
Take, for example, the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra*.
Exhort others to go to the Western Land to be reborn there according to their vows;
furthermore, wherever one may be reborn in a pure land,
encourage them to find contentment in Maitreya’s ascent to Tuṣita Heaven.
Alternatively, one may visualize Ākāśagarbha,
or again, visualize Samantabhadra and others; thus,
there are many appropriate times for such instruction.
It is not at fixed times such as the third or fifth watches;
for instance, according to the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, [the Buddha] was sometimes on the banks of the Gaṅgā River and so forth.
Since these are not fixed times, [it cannot be determined].

As for the *Mahāsaṃnipāta-sūtra* and other texts stating that it is "due to conditions" (*pratyaya*),

Because there are four conditions,

"Not by way of nature" means:

The provisional [teaching] is not a literal expression;

Furthermore, since the mind of principle is called the "nature-seed-lineage" (*prakṛti-bīja-gotra*), why can it not be said that one is called a bodhisattva by virtue of this nature? Since it is indeed by virtue of this nature, [it must be so].

Furthermore, this contradicts the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*,
as has already been cited previously.

Not so. Who says that ordinary beings lack the nature of an arhat and yet become arhats?

Furthermore, it says:

The World-Honored One teaches that the emptiness of phenomena is the *tathāgatagarbha*,

This is not the same as the non-Buddhists.
You maintain that the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) possesses a substantial entity (svabhāva), is eternal, and is capable of producing all things;
how does this differ from the non-Buddhist doctrines of primordial matter (prakṛti) and so forth?
If one maintains that an empty essence can give rise to all things,
it is identical to the theory of causelessness;
furthermore, it is the same as the Daoist view of Zhuangzi and Laozi, which holds that existence arises from non-existence.
If one maintains that permanent phenomena arise by taking [other things] as conditions,
this further contradicts the *Abhidharmasamuccaya*.
In the fourth chapter of the *Abhidharmasamuccaya*, which explains the characteristics of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*), it says:
"Because it arises dependently on impermanence.

for if that which is unarisen were the cause,
very few arisen phenomena could be established.
In the context of the meaning of dependent origination, it is said:

because their temporal duration is equal."
This refers to the meaning of the uninterrupted continuity of cause and effect.
Nor can it be said that this is explained based on the contaminated (*sāsrava*) or adventitious (*āgantuka*) nature;
for that treatise, in its discussion of forward and reverse contemplation, states:
One should contemplate the meaning of dependent origination in this way:

Because it does not exclude the untainted (anāsrava).

Furthermore, the treatise states:

Because it serves as the causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*) for both contaminated (*sāsrava*) and uncontaminated (*anāsrava*) phenomena respectively,
the substance of the eighth consciousness, being contaminated, cannot be the cause of the uncontaminated.
The *Sūtra of Immeasurable Meanings* states: "All dharmas arise from one dharma; that which is called 'one dharma' is the signless (*animitta*).
The *Great Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* says:

Furthermore, it is said:
"How could the 'self' (ātman) as described in the Sūtras be identical to the 'self' of those non-Buddhists?

The various Mahāyāna sūtras provisionally establish the names of the four virtues— permanence, bliss, self, and purity— with respect to their meaning; however,

One should not be like the non-Buddhists who reckon that eternal dharmas are the cause,

you, however, maintain that eternal dharmas are the cause.

how could there be any distinction?
This too is untenable.
The Nirvāṇa Sūtra says:
"Originally non-existent, now existent;
having existed, it returns to non-existence."
Taking this as evidence,
the meaning of that passage is different;
it does not state that there was originally nothing which now exists due to the absence of causes.
It is said that what was originally non-existent arises from causes;
thus it is said that what was originally non-existent now exists.
Once arisen, it immediately ceases; how then can it be said to return to non-existence?
If one adheres to the literal statement that "non-existence" implies the absence of causes, then once something has arisen, it must cease.
How, then, can you maintain that the Buddha’s *dharmakāya* is eternally abiding?
Furthermore, he asks himself:
"If a permanent dharma gives rise to an impermanent dharma,
why is it that in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*..."
The Buddha said to the non-Buddhist:
"Your cause is eternal,
but your fruit is impermanent."
"If the cause is impermanent, can the fruit be permanent?
He replied, "Causes are of two kinds: distant causes and proximate causes."
Fruits are categorized as proximate fruits and remote fruits.
Non-Buddhists possess only eternal causes but lack eternal fruits;
in the Buddha-dharma, the remote cause is eternal.
The proximate cause is impermanent;
the remote effect is permanent;
the proximate effect is impermanent.
This answer serves as a corrective standard.
The *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*, fascicle 33, states:
"All wholesome karma is the cause of nirvāṇa."
There are two kinds of causes:

Twenty-seventh: It is said that the cause of nirvāṇa is called buddha-nature;

As stated in [the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*] 22:
Before attaining anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi,

The fruit is not so;
some belong to the three periods of time, while others do not.
According to the meaning of this passage,
the cause consists of merit and wisdom,
while the fruit encompasses both wisdom and abandonment.
Therefore, the cause extends through the three periods of time,
while the fruit may belong to a period of time or not.
If one says that True Suchness (tathatā) is the remote cause, [it is so].
The cause also extends to both the mundane and the supramundane;
why, then, do you speak only of the three periods of time?
As it says in [Treatise] 33:
The buddha-nature of sentient beings is like empty space;
for it does not belong to the three periods of time,
as the buddha-nature is eternal.
It is not subsumed within the three periods of time.
Furthermore, the Buddha himself replied:
"I am conditioned by impermanence."
If the fruit were eternal,
there would be distinctions of distance and proximity within the cause;
the cause would thus pervade the three periods of time.
Now there are those who, from their ordinary minds, turn the Buddhist teachings upside down,
claiming that the distant cause is both permanent and impermanent,
and falsely correlating the near and distant causes and effects to divide them into the permanent and the impermanent.
Furthermore, you yourself admit that True Suchness gives rise to phenomena;
why then can it only give rise to them distantly as a remote cause (*parokṣa-hetu*),
while a cause cannot give rise to them proximately as an immediate cause (*sannikṛṣṭa-hetu*)?
Since suchness is eternally abiding,
it does not act as a cause in the near term,
nor is it empty in the distant term.
The essence of nature is quiescent and, while it can act as a cause from afar,
it is likewise so nearby;
for its essence is without differentiation between before and after.
The Buddha taught that the cause of arising is impermanent;
to claim it is permanent would contradict the Buddha’s teaching.
The Buddha possesses the nature of non-existence.

To contradict the teachings of the Sage while asserting that things possess intrinsic nature is to cling to one's own intellectual views as correct and to regard the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas as being wrong.
How is this different from waiting for a rabbit’s horn to touch Mount Sumeru,

Do you not reflect upon this? 4.

All are the same in this regard:

The Error of Taking True Suchness as the Seed. Fifth: Regarding the error of taking true suchness (*tathatā*) as the seed, there is an interpretation which states that the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* says:
From what seed do all supramundane dharmas arise?
If one says they arise from seeds whose intrinsic nature is heaviness (*dausthulya*),
that is not reasonable.
The answer is: All supramundane dharmas arise from seeds that have true suchness (*tathatā*) as their objective condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*);
they do not arise from seeds accumulated through the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of those [mundane dharmas].
There are two interpretations regarding this in the West (India).
First, Hufa and others say:
This is the wisdom that takes suchness as its object; because suchness serves as the objective condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*), it is called the seed of the objective condition of suchness.
The two, Nanda and others, say:
"These seeds of hearing-perfuming arise from the Buddha’s fundamental wisdom (mūla-jñāna) as the seeds for each respective object-condition (ālambana-pratyaya) of True Suchness (tathatā)."
These two interpretations are incorrect. Why is this?
The treatise states:
If they are not produced from seeds accumulated through habitual tendencies,
for what reason are the three types of individuals with the lineage for the dharma of nirvāṇa established?
And one establishes the person (pudgala) who lacks the nature for parinirvāṇa.
Why is this? Because all possess the suchness (tathatā) as their objective condition (ālambana-pratyaya).
According to the intent of this objection,
true suchness exists in all [beings] without any distinction of superiority or inferiority.
Question: For what reason are there three vehicles of spiritual capacity (*gotra*) and those with or without the nature [of awakening]?
This is not logically consistent.
Answer: The respondent answers that it is because not everyone possesses the seed of wisdom (*jñānabīja*).
The objector challenges [the position] by asserting that everything possesses *tathatā* (suchness).
This is because the method of challenging consists in restating and explaining the point of contention,
as they share the same textual basis.
Furthermore, the treatise itself provides a question-and-answer exchange.
It cannot be said that the opponent failed to grasp the meaning of the response;
therefore, we know that the respondent answered by taking *tathatā* (suchness) as the seed.
The critic immediately states that existence and non-existence cannot be different;
thus, we know that True Suchness (tathatā) can act as the seed for production.
This is consistent with the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, which states that although True Suchness gives rise to all phenomena...
As for the claim that "True Suchness is unarisen," this is also not the case. Why is that?
If dharmas were produced with true thusness as their seed,
the faults would be as previously stated:
it would constitute an unequal cause.
Regarding the claim made within the *Wangzhong* (The Refutation of Falsity) that the two masters’ commentaries contradict the treatise (*śāstra*),
this is also not the case; their commentaries do not contradict the treatise.

Why is this? The answer is: the seeds of the wisdom that takes True Suchness (*tathatā*) as its object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*) serve as the cause for supramundane phenomena (*lokottara-dharma*).
Since the intended meaning is that True Suchness (tathatā) serves as the object of cognition,
and since there are pervasive subjects of cognition,
it would follow that everything should likewise be established [as such].
For what reason can one establish the distinction between existence and non-existence?
If it were the case that true suchness itself acts as the seed capable of producing [phenomena],
then one should simply say that supramundane dharmas arise from the seeds of true suchness.
Why is it necessary to say that seeds arise from the true nature (*tathatā*) as their object-condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*)?
Vasubandhu’s *Prajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:
"If true nature were substantially existent at all times and in all places..."
Why is it that some people are able to attain [it] while others cannot?
The verse answers:
"Time and place truly exist."
Yet they do not attain true suchness;
lacking wisdom, they abide in phenomena.
Others, possessing wisdom, attain it.
The commentary says:
Why is it not attained?
Because that lack of wisdom causes the mind to dwell upon phenomena.
Because that [mind] is not pure,
and because the mind of one possessing wisdom does not dwell upon phenomena,
he is therefore able to attain it.
According to the intent of this treatise,
it clarifies that [the objection] is as pervasive as the analogy itself; thus,
it answers that objection by citing both types of cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) together.
If one clearly knows that the lineage (gotra) does not exist by its very nature (dharmatā), yet it were otherwise,
then one should simply cite the abiding dharma.
What need is there to speak of "wisdom"?
Therefore, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* distinguishes the five natures based on the presence of seeds for ultimate obstacles and the innate, naturally existing (*dharmatā-prakṛtistha*) untainted seeds.
In the *Prajñā-śāstra*, the objection is raised using the pervasiveness of suchness (*tathatā*);
the response is given by citing wisdom (*jñāna*) and its obscurations (*āvaraṇa*).
The *Yogācārabhūmi* addresses this by raising a comprehensive objection and providing a partial response regarding obstacles;
its intent is to clarify that there is a difference between those who possess and those who lack the seeds of wisdom.
It does not follow from the denial of dharmas.
If their natures were established as different on account of denying dharmas,
then one should simply establish the existence of nature.
The absence of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatā*) should not be divided into four types.
Furthermore, since the Mahāyāna permits the purification of the denial of the Dharma (*dharmāpavāda*) in every instance,
how could Maitreya not have known that it is ultimately impossible to sever?
Furthermore, those who slander the Dharma and commit the five heinous crimes (ānantarya-karma) incur retribution in the evil realms;
these are merely afflictive obscurations (kleśāvaraṇa).
Why then do you claim that there exists the seed of the cognitive obscuration (jñeyāvaraṇa) which is ultimately inexhaustible?
Regarding those seeds that are not afflictive obstructions and which reside in the basis (*āśraya*),
one portion is established as the *śrāvaka* lineage and another portion is established as the *pratyekabuddha* lineage.
How could it be that those of the two vehicles are called "without the seed-nature" merely because they slander the Dharma?
For it is admitted that those of the two vehicles attain the fruit of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa-phala*),
subsequently undergo the transformation of birth (*pariṇāmiki-jāti*), and turn their minds toward the Great Vehicle.
How could it be that the cognitive obscurations (jñeyāvaraṇa) can never be severed?
Furthermore, if one slanders the two kinds of emptiness, this constitutes the extreme of nihilism regarding the *Mahāyānasaṃparigraha-śāstra*,
whereby all roots of goodness are universally severed among the four types of such persons.
It is not that they lack causes altogether; rather,
it is not so, for [the roots of goodness] are universally severed externally.
Furthermore, what other karma is so heavy as to constitute an ultimate obstruction?
Moreover, if something is called an "obstruction" because it cannot be severed,
then it should be clearly identified and cited.
Why is it stated separately that there is ultimately no cause?
Furthermore, if True Suchness were the seed that directly gives rise to supramundane phenomena,
there would be, in brief, four faults.
First, there is the fault of internal contradiction between earlier and later statements. Previously,
in the section on the "Original Nature," it was stated that untainted states arise from tainted minds.
Now it is said that true thusness (tathatā) arises;
from what, then, would this definitely proceed?
These two positions are mutually contradictory.
Second, there is the fault of contradicting the sacred teachings.
In the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* and the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha*, regarding the meaning of seeds,
it is stated in all instances that they perish in a single moment.
Because it perishes immediately after arising,
no permanent phenomenon can constitute a seed,
as it would be without distinction at all times.
This is not possible.
The objection states:
"It is contrary to the nature of things (*dharmatā*) that seeds are perfumed by being associated with the perfuming agent."
How can it be called a "seed"?
It is not so; the meaning of "seed" is explained through seven senses.
The "perfuming agent" (kṣobhaka) and the "object perfumed" (kṣobhya) explain the meaning of perfuming (vāsanā).
Furthermore, it is taught that innate seeds (prakṛtistha-bīja) increase through perfuming;
it is not said that they are produced by perfuming.
To say that it arises through perfuming refers to newly perfumed seeds;
this entails the fault of contradicting three points of our own school's tenets.

To contradict the *Foxing lun* (Treatise on Buddha-nature) by asserting that "that which has substance gives rise to that which lacks substance" while claiming that True Suchness directly gives rise to supramundane phenomena,
one should instead say that "two things possessing substance give rise to that which possesses substance."
Why is it said to be one?
Because there would be the fault of contradiction between advancing and retreating.
If that which is with outflows were to give rise to that which is without outflows, [the sequence would be disrupted].
Furthermore, it contradicts the fifty-two [points] regarding the non-existence of the production of seeds from the specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) of the heavy residues (*dausthulya*);
there are even more faults,
as has already been demonstrated previously.
The remaining meanings should be understood by analogy with this.

The *Buddhadhātu-śāstra* states:

7. Regarding the seven errors concerning the arising of the outflow-free (anāsrava) from the outflows (āsrava), there is a meaning [to be explained].

That explanation is irrational;
this interpretation of the first reason contradicts itself from beginning to end.

First, this is contradictory.

This explains the contributory cause (pratyaya-hetu),
not the intrinsic nature (prakṛti).

According to the aforementioned scriptural passage:

there is a contradiction between these three characteristics.
It is further said:
"Just as although the earth can produce all things,
it must depend upon seeds as the direct cause."

its fundamental nature is likewise so,
depending upon the perfuming of hearing as its causal condition.
The Noble Path then arises.

the fundamental nature is the contributory cause.

Fourth, there is a contradiction.

The *Cheng weishi lun* (Treatise on the Establishment of Consciousness-Only) contains both ancient and new interpretations of heterodox masters;

Furthermore, it says:
The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states:

In the section on attaining accomplishment through understanding,

"Furthermore, although the supramundane mind has not yet arisen, it is called the 'supramundane mind'?"
Although it has not yet arisen,
it is already able to counteract the entanglements of the various afflictions;

If external [objects] were necessarily identical to internal [consciousness],
they would have to possess the four conditions and so forth.
Furthermore, it says:

The Supreme Mundane Dharma (*laukikāgradharma*) is a mundane cause and not a producer of supramundane seeds.
Furthermore, the untainted arises from causes that are untainted;
because the cause of the untainted is itself untainted, it is called "untainted.

Whose are these untainted seeds?

It is not the case that by disbelieving nirvāṇa one transforms ignorance into wisdom,

The treatise states that it refers only to the initial momentary [state] of the five untainted aggregates (*anāsrava-skandha*), and so forth.

8. Explaining the Error Regarding the Sequence of the Teaching. There is a meaning [to be understood] regarding the error concerning the sequence of the teaching:
the preceding sūtra’s gradual teaching spoke only of the four abodes as the cause of the three realms of existence.
Later, the *Śrīmālādevī-siṃhanāda-sūtra* clarifies that the five abidings are collectively taught as the root of birth and death:
because the four abidings are not severed, one undergoes the body of segmented existence;
because the abiding of ignorance persists, one attains the substance of transformation.
Because the Buddha’s teachings differ according to the sequence of their presentation,
the treatise explains that the Buddha’s sūtras do not contradict the timing of the instructions;
for example, as stated in the *Saṃdhinirmocana*, those taught prior to it are designated as the "earlier teaching."
The teachings following the Lotus Assembly constitute the subsequent teaching.
It does not fully realize that [the Buddha] spoke only of the indeterminate [turning of the mind], yet the inclination toward tranquility still exists as a real cessation;
one does not abandon the body within the three realms.

It does not separately explain the transformation of death (*pariṇāmi-maraṇa*); rather, it speaks only of the preservation of formations (*saṃskāra*) and the preservation of the segmented body (*kalala-deha*).
This is precisely what is found in the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra*, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, and other such texts.

After the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, those of both determinate and indeterminate natures all turn their minds [toward the Mahāyāna], such that there is no longer any real extinction for the two vehicles.
Having cast off the body of the triple world, they then receive the body of transformation;
this is not [a body] of the triple world.
The *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra*, the *Śrīmālādevī-siṃhanāda-sūtra*, the *Anuttarāśraya-sūtra*, the *Buddhadhātu-śāstra*, and so forth are such [texts].

The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* contains explicit textual evidence regarding its date forty years [after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa].
Furthermore, there is no sacred teaching stating that the *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra* and other such sutras appeared prior to it.
Moreover, the *Anuttaraśraya-sūtra* does not postdate the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.
How is this known? Before King Śreṇika had ascended to the throne of the kingdom,
there was already Bimbisāra.

In the *Anuttarāśrayasūtra*, among the listing of the assembly, it says:
"Bimbisāra was the foremost. Judging by this, one may know that [this sūtra] is not posterior to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*.

The sūtra says:

Candraprabha had already long placed his faith in the Buddha.
The Śrīmālā-sūtra states:
"He had not long believed in the Buddha.
This indicates that it was composed prior to the *Benevolent Kings Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*.
That is not so. It has already been twenty-nine years since I heard this sutra;
how then could it be said in the Śrīmālādevī Sūtra that my faith in the Buddha is not yet long-standing?
Based on this, one knows that it is not after the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.
Furthermore, according to the *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra*, as stated by the Tripiṭaka Master Bodhiruci:
"Moreover, it relies upon the [first] council."
In the first year, he preached the Mahāsaṃnipāta-ratnaketu-dhāraṇī and the Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra;

Therefore, I have posed this question.

Since that fixed sequence of before and after is likewise based on nothing but empty space,

Furthermore, there are many other faults.
What are these faults? To begin with, it is said:
Although the preceding sutra states that those of the two vehicles truly enter nirvana,

No; the *Laṅkāvatāra* states that those who fall into the transformation-death (*pariṇāmi-cyuti*) yet are capable of proceeding toward the Great [Vehicle] possess an indeterminate nature (*aniyata-gotra*).
How is this known? According to the seventh [chapter], it says:

You have even said that they are not yet able to realize the dharmas of the first stage.”
How much more so regarding the gate of the bliss of quiescence in the eighth stage?
The Buddha told Mahāmati:
"There are three kinds of śrāvakas."
Regarding the statement "entering the gate of the bliss of quiescence in the eighth stage":
this refers to those who were previously practitioners of the bodhisattva path but have fallen into the stage of the śrāvakas.
Returning to rely on the fundamental mind to cultivate the bodhisattva practices,
they enter together with them through the gate of the bliss of cessation in the eighth stage;
they are not śrāvakas of cessation who possess overweening pride.
Because they are unable to enter the bodhisattva practice,
they have never realized that the three realms are mind-only,
nor have they ever cultivated the various dharmas of a bodhisattva.
Because they have never practiced the various pāramitās or the conduct of the ten stages,
śrāvakas who are fixed in their determination for cessation cannot realize that gate of the bliss of cessation practiced by bodhisattvas.
Furthermore, a verse states:
"Those śrāvakas who are fixed in their destiny do not practice the bodhisattva path;
they enter together with others into the eighth stage."
Because this is the fundamental bodhisattva,
by analogy with this,
it is the indeterminate vehicle among the five vehicles.
The intent of the *Dharmapada-yoga* is entirely the same.
Furthermore, the eighth [chapter] asks:
"How is it that the Buddha, the World-Honored One, bestows predictions upon the great Arhats and others?"
The Buddha replied: "Mahāmati,
for those śrāvakas who have previously practiced the bodhisattva path,
I bestow the prediction of enlightenment based upon their attainment of nirvana without remainder."
Mahāmati, I bestow predictions of enlightenment upon the śrāvakas in order to inspire courage in those beings who are timid and weak.
Mahāmati, this applies both to this world and to other buddha-fields.
There are sentient beings who practice the bodhisattva path yet take pleasure in the vehicle of the śrāvakas; for their sake,
the Buddha turns them away from that [preference].
One attains great bodhi.
The verse says:
"The three vehicles and that which is not a vehicle."
The Buddhas have immeasurable vehicles;
they bestow all prophecies regarding the stage of Buddhahood and declare the severance of all afflictions.
Realizing noble wisdom within one's own body and attaining nirvana without remainder,
he encourages those sentient beings who are timid and weak.
Therefore, it is taught through intentional concealment (*saṃdhāya-bhāṣita*). By this principle,
it corresponds exactly to the explanation of the three types of mind-made bodies (*manomaya-kāya*) as set forth in the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra*.
Those from the first bhūmi upward are determined to proceed toward quiescence;
since they have not yet realized the gate of the bliss of quiescence practiced by bodhisattvas,
it is clear that they cannot attain the mind-made body (manomayakāya).
It is a fault because one cannot know [this].
Furthermore, it is said that the *Amoghapāśa Sūtra* and the *Saṃgha Sūtra* state:
The Śuddhāvāsakāyika devas all set out for the Great [Vehicle].
This is judged to be the teaching following the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*;
however, it is not yet known on what basis this is understood.
The scriptural teaching is indeed consistent; however,
since there is no explicit proof for it,
how can one suppress this fact and pass judgment?
Furthermore, it is said:
"The assertions of both masters of the Vijñaptimātra school are both illogical;
therefore, we know that before the assembly at the Lotus Sūtra, none of the sages had yet resolved their minds toward enlightenment."
After the assembly at the Lotus Sutra, those in the Śuddhāvāsa heavens also set it forth.
The masters of the Vijñaptimātratā school contradict the sutras in establishing their tenets,
asserting that there are not merely one or two [realms].
That is not so. How can one explain that the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra* was taught before the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, as they themselves admit?
Furthermore, it is only the *Saṃdhinirmocana-sūtra* that was taught in a pure land.
The characteristics of the Pure Land are explained;
the assembly is enumerated and their virtues praised as being identical to the stage of Buddhahood.
Regarding the "explanation of the meaning as it truly is" (*yathārthārtha*), the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra* provides the commentary.
All of these are śrāvakas of indeterminate lineage who, having attained the lesser fruit, proceed toward great bodhi;
therefore, they are called "great. This applies unless their minds have not been turned [toward enlightenment].
They do not contemplate the Pure Land.
Furthermore, the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* and other texts explain the One Vehicle through ten meanings, stating that it refers to those of indeterminate lineage;
thus, it is held that both those in training (*śaikṣa*) and those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) are permitted to turn their minds [toward the Mahāyāna].
Furthermore, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* (Dazhidu lun), in its commentary on the two teachings of the *Pañcaviṃśati-sāhasrikā-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra* and the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*,
states: "There are three kinds of people who possess a wondrous and pure land that transcends the triple world,
such that even the name of affliction does not exist therein."
In this land, one hears the Lotus Sūtra from the Buddha and completes the path to Buddhahood.
How could it be that all the holy ones do not resolve their minds [to attain enlightenment] upon hearing the preaching of the Lotus Sūtra?
Furthermore, it is said:
"The *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* clearly states that those of fixed nature who have attained quiescence still undergo death through transformation (*pariṇāmikī-maraṇa*).
Both scripture and reasoning make this evident."
How can one insist that the former teachings were not spoken in the later sutras?
This is also not the case. To admit this, let us refer to the fourth fascicle of the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*, which says:

Mahāmati, because Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas have not yet realized the selflessness of phenomena (dharmanairātmya) and have not yet attained the inconceivable transformation-body birth (nirmāṇakāya-janman),
I have taught the path of the One Vehicle (ekayāna) for the sake of those Śrāvakas.
This is called "not yet attained.
Furthermore, based on what text does it say that those who have attained certainty (niyata-pudgala) clearly receive the transformation body (nirmāṇakāya)?
According to the meaning of this text:
A person of indeterminate nature who has not yet heard the Mahāyāna cannot undergo transformation;
how then could it be permitted that one who is determinedly incapable of turning their mind could receive transformation?
Furthermore, this same scriptural passage also states:
"They have not yet departed from inconceivable transformation-death," and it also says:
[as previously cited].
One cannot be free from inconceivable death by transformation (*acintya-nirmāṇa-maraṇa*).
There is also a version which says:
"One has not yet attained freedom from inconceivable death by transformation."
There are no explicit passages that provide a definitive teaching; thus,
those of fixed nature find it easy to receive [the teaching].
It is also stated in the second [chapter]:
"Because they fall into the inconceivable death of transformation.
This explains that after their minds have been turned back toward awakening, they fall into the inconceivable birth-and-death of transformation.
There is no definitive textual passage that establishes transformation (*pariṇāma*).
Furthermore, if one were to admit that the body born of transformation is itself the body of feeling (*vedanā*),
how could it be said that such [attainments] constitute the entry into the selflessness of persons (*pudgala-nairātmya*) and even the generation of the mind that constitutes *nirvāṇa*?
Ordinary beings undergo the body of segmented birth and death, knowing it as such;
sages undergo the body of transformation.
How could one grasp this as *nirvāṇa*? To claim that there is "having remainder" (*sopadhiśeṣa*) is not [correct],
because it is not known that the obstacles to knowledge (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) persist even when other [afflictions] have been eliminated.
He himself does not grant this;
that is to say, for one who has a remaining support (sopadhiśeṣa) to turn the mind toward the Mahāyāna,
it is necessary to first abandon the fragmented existence (bheda-deha).
They undergo a different kind of transformation and attain the bliss of samādhi,
which they mistakenly believe to be nirvana without remainder.
It is also like one who, having heard little of the Dharma, attains the fourth dhyāna and considers it the ultimate fruit;
even when seeing the signs of death, such a person still gives rise to a mind of slander.
How much less could a sage, seeing that sensations undergo transformation and change,
consider them to be "without remainder"?
Furthermore, this is consistent with the texts concerning the Five Vehicles.
In the first two vehicles, there is no mention of entering the Mahāyāna;
it is only in the fourth, the indeterminate vehicle, that it says:
"Mahāmati, those three kinds of persons are free from the obstacle of afflictions."
Because they attain purification through perfuming,
they perceive non-self;
because they attain the gateway to the bliss of samādhi.
Śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas ultimately realize the dharmakāya of the Tathāgata.
As for those three types of persons,
they are the three types found among those of indeterminate vehicle.
This does not refer to the first three vehicles mentioned previously.
If that were the case,
one would have to separately designate them as a fourth vehicle.
Alternatively, it may be that the first three vehicles— both those of determinate and indeterminate nature— are all included in the explanation,
while the fourth person refers exclusively to those of indeterminate nature;
thus, it speaks of "those three types."
This refers to those of indeterminate nature among the aforementioned three. Otherwise,
it would mean that all three— those of determinate and indeterminate natures— are admitted to enter the Great Vehicle.
This contradicts what is stated in the seventh and eighth [sections] below,
as already cited previously;
there is no explicit textual statement that those of fixed nature (niyata-gotra) who have attained quiescence undergo death through transformation (pariṇāmi-cyuti).
It is a fault because the principles of the teaching are clearly contradicted by empty words.
Furthermore, it is asked within the dialogue:
"For what reason do these two explanations differ?"
The answer states:
As it is said in the sūtras,
the royal palace has not yet been described as being the transformation body (nirmāṇakāya) of a Buddha.
When propagating the teachings of this period,
he taught that Buddhahood is attained through thirty-four moments of mind,
yet he did not speak of the *ālayavijñāna*.
In propagating the teachings of this period,
[the Master] stated that the meditative attainment of cessation exists only in the desire and form realms,
and asserted that the seeds depend upon both matter and mind.
When propagating the later teachings,
its meaning was modified according to the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*;

Forty years later, you will realize that these two types of cessation are not ultimate.
You will possess the ālayavijñāna and fall into the inconceivable death and rebirth of the transformation-body (nirmāṇa-kāya).
As for the claim that at the time of propagating this sutra,
the treatises followed the teaching accordingly,
this is also not the case.

the meditative absorption of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti) relies upon the bodies of the desire and form realms.

Furthermore, the previous thesis that the seeds depend upon the eighth consciousness and so forth has been revised; it is now held that,

these [seeds] are likewise indeterminate and lack substantial reality.
The *Nirvāṇa-jñāna-śāstra* and the *Fodi-jingyanlun* both state that there is "transformative birth and death" (*pariṇāmika-jarāmaraṇa*).
In what sense do they differ?
To judge the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra*, and others as teachings from the first forty years [of the Buddha’s life]—
as was previously cited— is incorrect in its distinction between earlier and later periods;
it fails to understand their commonality and does not recognize that they are not different.
It is a fault because it is seen as being different from [the other].
Furthermore, it is said that the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicle 80, speaks of two types of nirvāṇa.
Because the ripening consciousness (vipākavijñāna) is devoid of grasping, the evolving consciousnesses (pravṛttivijñāna) and so forth can no longer arise;
there remains only that which is pure,
unconditioned (asaṃskṛta), and free from defilement.
The true dharma-realm exists;
as stated in the Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra, one should extinguish all marks and not grasp at future objects— this is the bliss of samādhi.
The followers of the Two Vehicles claim this is nirvāṇa,
but it is not so; furthermore, what is taught in that sūtra is inconsistent from beginning to end.
The second fascicle explains that Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, fearing the suffering of the delusive thoughts of birth and death, seek nirvāṇa;
for they do not know that there is no distinction between the world and nirvāṇa.
Discriminating all phenomena as either dharmas or non-dharmas,

Those who falsely grasp at this as *nirvāṇa* are the persons of the two vehicles who are still in training (*śaikṣa*) and ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*).
Clinging to the state of those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), they take that which is attained after the cessation of the sense faculties— the remainderless state (*anupadhiśeṣa*)— to be the ultimate.

Therefore, Mahāmati, those foolish people constantly revolve and do not rest within the wheel of birth and death in the world;

Regarding those of definitive nature who extinguish the sense faculties and so forth:
both body and cognition are extinguished, and only *tathatā* (suchness) remains.
As the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* states:
Only when the perceptions of mind are extinguished does one attain the dharma of quiescence.

Regarding the "joy of samādhi," this is explained in the text of the seventh fascicle:
those of indeterminate nature who turn their minds toward the Mahāyāna attain entry into the various stages (*bhūmi*).
Speaking according to their original names,
they are identical to bodhisattvas of sudden enlightenment who attain the meditative absorption of cessation within the various stages.
It is named "The Dharma Gate of Falling into the Joy of Samādhi. How is this known?
For it asks and answers itself as follows:

If these followers of the two vehicles cast off their coarse分段 (fen-duan) bodies and abide in samādhi, [they attain this].

For the sake of generating the aspiration for bodhi,
the roots of goodness, the false roots of goodness, and the Arhats who manifest as Arhats for the purpose of transformation—

It is taught that those who have attained definitive quiescence are śrāvaka arhats,

one knows that for those of fixed nature who enter the nirvāṇa without remainder, there is only true suchness (tathatā).

If one dwells in the bliss of samādhi and conceives the notion that this is nirvāṇa,

It is further stated:
"Briefly, there are thirteen points of difference between the former and latter teachings.
First, it says:

If one is free from all faults and,

Answer: According to the *Vajra-uttarāsvāda-dhāraṇī-sūtra*, Mañjuśrī said:

If there is no ignorance, then there is no birth.
If there is no birth, then there is no defilement.
Mañjuśrī, awakening is undefiled.
Because its nature is pure and its essence is radiant,
Mañjuśrī, seeing this matter, I speak of ignorance;
thus it is spoken of as non-dual.
By analogy with this,

because this purity is non-dual.

This is clarified by two verses in the *Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra*.
The first says:
Since there are no phenomena existing apart from the nature of phenomena (dharmatā),

"Afflictions are themselves awakening.

Furthermore, a verse says:

Having understood this,
one is liberated from greed; therefore,

This may be understood by analogy.
Among the various sūtras and śāstras of these three aforementioned categories,

Alternatively, it may be explained comprehensively,

As it says in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, fascicle 22:
Some say that faith in bodhi is the cause.

Alternatively, one may emphasize the preeminent causes with respect to the resultant state,

Alternatively, both principle and phenomena may be manifested together,
as stated in the seventh fascicle of the Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra,
where the Buddha addressed Mahāmati:
The Tathāgatagarbha is the cause of both the wholesome and the unwholesome;

Just as the waves of the great ocean are never interrupted because they arise simultaneously with the body,

Furthermore, it is said:
"Mahāmati, the Tathāgatagarbha-ālayavijñāna does not reside within the ālaya;

"The Tathāgatagarbha-ālayavijñāna is neither born nor extinguished.
This explains the principle.
Furthermore, the eighth [consciousness] says:
The ālayavijñāna is called the empty tathāgatagarbha.
Because it is not permeated by the mental formations of the evolving consciousnesses (pravṛttivijñāna), it is designated as "empty."
Being fully endowed with the dharmas of untainted perfuming is called "not empty";
this is the nature of right practice.
The *Śrīmālādevī-sūtra* states that there are two kinds of *tathāgatagarbha*:

The treasury of all afflictions is identical to the *tathāgatagarbha* as emptiness in the *Laṅkāvatāra*.
World-Honored One, the non-empty *tathāgatagarbha* transcends the sands of the Ganges, being inseparable, non-detached, and non-different [from it].
Regarding the inconceivable Buddha-dharma,
the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* states:

Furthermore, because it is fully permeated by untainted dharmas (*anāsravadharma*),

It continues, saying:

As stated in the fourth chapter of the *Ratnagotravibhāga*:
"There are two aspects of buddha-nature.

Second, it is like the fruit of a tree:
the element (dhātu) from beginningless time,

Practicing the unsurpassed path,

Furthermore, it cites a verse which says:
"The nature that has existed since beginningless time..."

The following is the explanation.
As for what is called "nature" (prakṛti),
it is like that of the Noble Ones (ārya).
The Śrīmālā-sūtra states:
"World-Honored One, when the Tathāgata speaks of the Tathāgatagarbha,

Below, it is also explained according to phenomena, saying:
In this way, to see and know as it truly is which afflictions are absent in which locations is called the knowledge of emptiness (*śūnyatājñāna*).

The meanings do not contradict one another when explained according to the distinctions between nature and characteristics, as well as the basis for the processes of transmigration and cessation.
Furthermore, this is the "Section Revealing the Essence" from the *Buddhadhātu-śāstra*.
The Tathāgatagarbha Section elucidates the three tathāgatagarbhas.
First is the "encompassing garbha," as stated below:
Because no sentient being whatsoever can ever transcend the realm of suchness (tathatā),

According to this, the *Laṅkāvatāra* [sūtra] refers to the out-flowing consciousness (*āsrava-vijñāna*) as the cause of birth and death.
Second, that which is concealed and hidden;

When the Tathāgata-nature abides prior to the path,

This is precisely the Śrīmālā’s "empty Tathāgatagarbha.
Third, as for its being a storehouse because it can encompass:
This refers to all the qualities exceeding the sands of the Ganges on the stage of fruition;

Furthermore, the "Chapter on the Three Causes" also encompasses both principle and phenomena. It states:
"The essence of Buddha-nature is of three kinds."
The meaning should be understood as being subsumed within the three natures.
As for these three types:
What are called the three causes are the three kinds of Buddha-nature.
As for the three causes:
First, the cause of attainment;
second, the cause of application;
third, the cause of fulfillment.
Suchness is the cause for that which is to be attained;
the bodhicitta is the cause of application;
and the bodhicitta along with the actions it initiates are the causes of fulfillment.
The perfection of causes refers to the perfection of the fruits of the practices of merit and wisdom; that is to say,
the qualities of knowledge (*jñāna*), abandonment (*prahāṇa*), and grace (*anugraha*).
Furthermore, it reveals the categories of essence;
the "Chapter on the Three Natures" explains the three natures and the three non-natures,
which exhaustively encompass the Tathāgata-garbha.
This [interpretation] is the most comprehensive and pervasive. If one takes the thirty-sixth [point],
both the causes and effects of defilement and purity in nirvana are collectively termed "Buddha-nature."
Therefore, the Sūtra says:
"These seven types of sentient beings,
if they possess wholesome dharmas..."
Whether it be unwholesome dharmas,
the path of application,
or the path of liberation.
Whether it be the path of succession,
its cause, or its fruit,
all are the Buddha-nature.
This is called the Tathāgata’s speech according to his own intention,
as explained according to the preceding meaning.
However, one should consider the cause for attaining [the fruit] in relation to the *nirmāṇakāya* and *sambhogakāya*.
It can be understood as being produced from them;

If one follows the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*,

Because suchness exists, there can be the manifestation of transformation-bodies (nirmāṇakāya),

If one regards it from the perspective of the *dharmakāya*,

As the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states:
It has other-nature as its cause,

However, it is called the cause for attaining the fruit because such a cause exists; for by virtue of this,

"Although it is not yet manifest,"
It must necessarily be manifestable;

When Śrīmālā is within the *saṃkleśa* (the enveloping sheaths), it is called the *tathāgatagarbha*.

Because it is capable of being manifested;

The *Buddhadhātu-śāstra* states:

Faith and aspiration, understood in terms of applied practice (*prayoga*), serve as the *janaka-hetu* (generating cause).

"The essence of nirvāṇa is not produced by these five causes."
Furthermore, there are two kinds of causes: the producing cause and the revealing cause.

The Dharma-body and nirvāṇa differ in meaning but are identical in essence.
Thus, one knows that True Suchness, in relation to the Dharma-body, is not the producing or revealing cause;
