2. Regarding the two non-dualities of existence and non-existence: if one discusses the nature of reality (*dharmatā*), there is no duality and nothing arises, as stated in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, fascicle 26.
Because even icchantikas who have severed their roots of goodness possess them as well.
That sutra states:
"If the bodhicitta were the Buddha-nature..."
Those who are icchantikas cannot truly be called icchantikas,
nor can the bodhicitta be called impermanent;
this is because the bodhicitta is not, in principle, the Buddha-nature.
If it is the case that those of the icchantika nature do not sever [the roots of goodness],
this has been sincerely taught in various places;
there is no need for extensive citation.
If one discusses the nature of practice,
there are further two kinds:
namely, the contaminated (sāsrava) and the uncontaminated (anāsrava).
The existence or non-existence of these two types of nature is not fixed.
If they possess the nature of being with outflows (*sāsrava*), the seeds of all sentient beings are certainly present;
as for their actual manifestation (*samudācāra*), it may or may not occur.
If it refers to the untainted [dharmas] in terms of their active manifestation (*samudācāra*),
then ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) do not possess them; however, if it refers to them in terms of their seeds (*bīja*), [they do].
There are those that are accomplished and those that are not.
As stated in the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicle 57:
"Regarding birth in the hells (*naraka*), the seeds and active manifestations (*samudācāra*) of eight faculties are necessarily accomplished."
Excluding the remaining three, eight, or [other] faculties, whether they are manifest or not,
the seeds of the three faculties are necessarily present,
while their manifestation is necessarily absent.
The seeds may be either accomplished or unaccomplished;
that is to say, those who possess the nature for parinirvāṇa accomplish them,
while those who do not possess the nature for parinirvāṇa do not accomplish them.
This is based on what currently exists;
if it were discussed in terms of what is yet to come,
that too would be manifest.
What is meant by "definite" and "indefinite"?
The *Anuttarāśrayasūtra*, the *Buddhadhātuśāstra*, and the *Ratnagotravibhāga* all state that there are three types of sentient beings.
First is attachment to existence (*bhava*).
Attachment to existence is further divided into two types:
the first is turning one's back on the path to *nirvāṇa*.
They lack the nature of nirvāṇa;
they do not seek nirvāṇa,
but instead aspire to and delight in saṃsāra.
The *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* (She da cheng lun), fascicle 14, states:
"If sentient beings lack the nature of nirvāṇa,
it is called 'the deficiency of causes.'"
Within this stage, the Buddhas are unable to cause them to enter parinirvāṇa,
nor do they possess mastery over their supernormal powers (abhijñā).
They lack the nature of nirvāṇa;
that is to say, they are attached to saṃsāra and do not have faith or delight in the Mahāyāna.
Unlike those who perform actions whose resulting fruits are determined, [they are not fixed].
Because they cannot be transformed during these two periods,
it is said that they lack the nature of *nirvāṇa* and do not attain mastery in this state.
Thus, they would eternally lack the nature of nirvāṇa.
Furthermore, the *Buddhatva-śāstra* states:
"Because the purified aspect serves as the condition and the pure nature serves as the cause, this contemplation is established."
It is not without causes and conditions.
If one were to contemplate the absence of causes and conditions without relying on these two factors,
it would be like the icchantika, who lacks the nature for nirvāṇa.
One ought to attain this contemplation;
however, since icchantikas lack this contemplation,
it is known that it must necessarily manifest only through the contemplation of causes and conditions.
The *Ratnagotravibhāga* is the same.
Furthermore, the third chapter of the *Ratnagotravibhāga* states:
"The Buddha-nature as the primary cause performs two kinds of functions for sentient beings in the indeterminate group."
First, because one sees the world and becomes weary of suffering;
second, because one sees nirvāṇa and yearns for its peace and bliss.
It is not said that those in the group of the wrongly fixed (mithyātva-niyata-rāśi) can perform these two functions.
The *Buddhatva-śāstra* is likewise the same.
The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* also states:
"One cannot establish the bodhicitta of an icchantika."
It is, for example, like a vajra being unable to destroy the horns of a white sheep and so forth,
as cited extensively above.
The ninth [chapter] says:
Furthermore, the Buddha said: "Good son, with the exception of the icchantikas, all other sentient beings,
having heard this sutra, will all be able to create the causes and conditions for roots of goodness."
Those into whose pores the light of the sound of the Dharma enters will certainly attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi;
since it is said that icchantikas will not attain it, [this light does not enter them].
It clarifies that there are those who lack Buddha-nature.
Furthermore, in the thirty-third fascicle of the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*,
it clarifies that among the seven kinds of people within the river of birth and death, there are those who lack it.
If there are these seven kinds of sons of good family,
either one person may possess all seven,
or there may be seven people, each possessing one.
Since it has already been stated that each is one,
those who are perpetually submerged are those without nature (niḥsvabhāva). If this were not so, [it would be contradictory].
How does this differ from [the case of] a single person possessing all seven?
The *Śīla-sūtra*, the *Bodhisattvabhūmi* of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, and the *Bodhisattvabhūmi* all state:
"Those without nature (asattva) lack the spiritual lineage (*gotra*), and so forth."

The *Śrāvakabhūmi*, the *Viniścayasaṃgrahaṇī*, the *Abhidharmasamudaya*, the *Buddhabhūmivyākhyāna*, and other such treatises all establish the existence and non-existence of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*);
this is explained in detail therein.
I shall not cite it in full here.
The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, fascicle 26, states:
"Good son, although I have said that all sentient beings possess Buddha-nature..."
Sentient beings do not understand such intentional speech of the Buddha as this.
Good son, even Bodhisattvas in their final birth cannot understand such speech,
let alone those of the two vehicles or other Bodhisattvas.
Furthermore, it is said:
"If one says that all sentient beings possess Buddha-nature,
this is called the Tathāgata’s speech according to his own intention."
The Tathāgata speaks thus according to his own intention;

The commentary states:
"Having no beginning" means that the nature-attained prajñā, great compassion, meditative concentration, and dharmakāya are all inherently present from the outset.
It is said that there is no beginning.
If that which is untainted (anāsrava) were to arise from that which is tainted (sāsrava),
then causes such as prajñā, great compassion (mahākaruṇā), and meditative concentration (dhyāna) would be dharmas with a beginning.
How can it be that there is no beginning [to this] and it arises from the outflows (*āsrava*)?
What is meant by "attainment by nature" (*prakṛti-pratilambha*)? The *Ratnagotravibhāga*, chapter four, states:
There are two aspects of Buddha-nature:
first, it is like the earth and its treasures;
second, it is like the fruit of a tree.
According to the meaning of that text,
Kṣitigarbha is a metaphor for *tathatā* (suchness),
while the tree and its fruit are metaphors for *prajñā* (wisdom) and so forth.
Therefore, it is said next:
based on the first simile, one knows that there is the primary dharmakāya;
based on the second simile, one knows that there are two buddha-bodies.
Both types of Buddha-nature are described as being without beginning throughout the world;
it is not yet clarified that they are inherently present as untainted (*anāsrava*) and not merely newly produced.
Furthermore, if the untainted seeds were produced solely as new entities,
then the taintful perfuming of hearing would serve as the direct causal condition for supramundane right view.
As stated in the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* translated by Paramārtha:
"The Buddha, the World-Honored One, said:
'From hearing the voice of another...'"
And through right reflection for oneself;
by these two causes,
right view arises.
The commentary states:
In the category of purification, right view is the foremost.
By what dharma does this right view serve as a dominant condition?
That is to say, hearing the voice from another and one's own correct reflection—
these two causes constitute the dominant conditions for right view.
It continues until it says:
"By these two causes, right view arises.
These two causes serve as the dominant conditions (*adhipatipratyaya*) for right view."
What is now referred to as "cause" (hetu) is a general term;
it is precisely the condition (pratyaya) that is being called the cause.
Furthermore, the treatise states:
The mundane mind is associated with right intention;
the supramundane pure mind is associated with right view.
At no time do they arise together or cease together.
The commentary states:
Right thought and right cultivation of wisdom arise from the four foundations of mindfulness;
the "Supreme Mundane Dharmas" constitute their stage.
This mind has not yet realized and seen the Four Truths;
therefore, it is called a mundane mind.
Once it has realized and seen the Four Truths, [it is no longer mundane].
Therefore, it is called supramundane.
It is a dharma free from intrinsic nature,
a dharma attained through cultivation.
Therefore, it is called the pure mind.
Right view is the first factor among the eightfold noble path.
This right view is inseparable from the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment.
It continues until it says:
"Because they arise from the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment,
one attains transcendence."
Since beginningless time,
there has been no sense of simultaneous arising and simultaneous ceasing between the mundane and supramundane minds,
because their natures are mutually contradictory.
The treatise says:
For this reason, the worldly mind is not perfumed by the pure mind; since there is no perfuming, [the pure mind does not exist].
It cannot be established as the seed for supramundane [attainment].
The commentary states:
If the wisdom born of reflection (*cintāmayī-prajñā*) were perfumed by a supramundane mind...
It could then be established as the seed for supramundane [attainments].
Since it lacks the quality of being perfumed,
the status of being a supramundane seed is not established.
According to this treatise,
if untainted seeds (*anāsrava-bīja*) are newly perfumed,
they can only arise once they are conjoined with the untainted [state].
Since there is no untainted (anāsrava) state prior to the path of seeing (darśanamārga),
how can the tainted (sāsrava) be perfumed to produce the untainted?
If you grant that the tainted perfumes the seeds of the untainted, [how can this be so?]
One should not challenge others [on this point].
It is not the case that seeds cannot be perfumed by those associated with the untainted (*anāsrava*),
for you yourself admit that untainted seeds are perfumed by that which is not associated with the untainted.
Question: If the impure (sāsrava) cultivation through hearing prior to the path of seeing cannot produce the outflow-free (anāsrava), how can the treatise state:
"Although it is a mundane dharma, it brings about a supramundane mind"?
The commentary states:
Although the mental consciousness is a mundane phenomenon, it is as follows.
One is able to penetrate the suchness of the four truths;
because it counteracts the obscurations of the four truths,
one achieves the supramundane mind.
The perfuming of hearing is likewise;
although it is a mundane phenomenon,
both its cause and its fruit are supramundane phenomena.
It also accomplishes the supramundane mind.
The answer is that because it is fundamentally untainted (*anāsrava*), subtle, hidden, and difficult to know,
it relies upon the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*) of tainted (*sāsrava*) habitual perfuming (*vāsanā*).
This reveals the originally existing untainted seeds;
these very seeds, during the stage of perfuming,
are also termed "perfuming through hearing."
Therefore, the subsequent treatise asks:
"For what reason?
The commentary explains:
Why is this? Because this Dharma is exclusively supramundane;
it is not a mundane dharma.
Because there are four kinds of remedies.
According to this principle,
since it is stated that these are exclusively supramundane and not mundane dharmas.
It clarifies that these are not out-flowing (sāsrava).
Furthermore, the treatise states:
"When this seed has not yet given rise to the supramundane pure mind..."

Based on this, it should be understood that the stage of permeation by outflows (*sāsrava-vāsanā*) occurs prior to the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*), as it serves as the antidote (*pratipakṣa*) to all afflictions of the higher mind.
There already exists the seed of the untainted mind (*anāsrava-citta*).
Furthermore, it is said that the seed is precisely the perfuming of hearing (*śruta-vāsanā*).
The faculty of "the root of the desire to know what is not yet known" in a bodhisattva is called the supramundane pure mind.
Prior to the arising of this mind, there exists the permeation of hearing.
This belongs to the stage of wisdom derived from hearing and reflection;
within the stages of hearing and reflection,
one should know this by analogy.
As for the statement that the perfuming of the out-flowing (sāsrava) [seeds] produces the supramundane mind,
this is explained from the perspective of the dominant condition (adhipatipratyaya); furthermore, it is explained in detail therein.
I shall not cite further examples here.
Question: Since all sentient beings equally possess *tathatā* (suchness) and the eighth consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*), why do you not allow these to be the direct cause for Buddhahood?
Answer: As previously clarified, just as [a cause] does not arise from itself, it likewise does not directly act as the primary cause for the arising of a phenomenon.
If it is admitted that the eighth consciousness is the direct cause of Buddhahood,
it must be untainted (anāsrava);
furthermore, it would then serve as the antidote to the tainted eighth consciousness.
Only then can one attain Buddhahood.
If you grant that the eighth consciousness is the direct cause for Buddhahood,
it must then be capable of counteracting its own eighth consciousness.
If that were so, it would contradict the *Viniścayasaṃgrahaṇī* of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* (Liang translation), which asks:
"How can the retributive consciousness containing all seeds become the cause of the impure category?
If it can act as the cause for supramundane pure minds that serve as remedies against defilement..."
The commentary states:
If one establishes that the fundamental consciousness (ālayavijñāna) is the supramundane cause that serves as the specific antidote to defilement,
then one cannot regard the fundamental consciousness as the cause of the impure category.
The category of impurity consists of the Truth of Origination and the Truth of Suffering.
Because it contains the seeds of karma and afflictions, it is the Truth of Origination.
It continues until it says:
Since it has already been established as the antidote to defilement and turbidity, and as the cause for supramundane mind,
it should not further be described as the cause for the category of the impure. By this same principle, [the same applies to the others].
The eighth [consciousness], being with outflows (*sāsrava*), is not the direct cause for Buddhahood.
Furthermore, this eighth consciousness is possessed by all alike;
there is no distinction between the three vehicles (*triyāna*).
This clarifies the distinct causes for the stages of good precepts (*śīla-bhūmi*) and the stages of bodhisattvas (*bodhisattva-bhūmi*),
as well as the distinctions among the three vehicles (*triyāna-gotra*) within the context of their training. Regarding these distinctions among the three vehicles:
Since all [phenomena] are established as impure,
they depend upon the originally non-outflowing seeds within this consciousness;
these are the true cause of Buddhahood.
Question: If you do not accept that *tathatā* (suchness) is the direct cause (*hetu-pratyaya*) of Buddhahood,
how can the *Buddhadhātu-śāstra* state that the principle of *tathatā* is the direct cause of Buddhahood,
while faith in the *Prajñāpāramitā* and so forth are the contributory causes (*pratyaya-hetu*)?
The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* further states that [consciousness] arises from seeds which have suchness as their objective condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*).
The answer is that these two scriptural passages have already been reconciled as before;
now they shall be explained once more.

Regarding the statement that "that which arises from seeds having True Suchness as its objective condition" (ālambana-pratyaya), this is a figurative way of saying that the objective condition itself is the seed;
in reality, True Suchness is not a seed for any conditioned phenomena.
As it is said that faith in the *prajñāpāramitā* and so forth constitute the seeds of the four virtues,
the four virtues of the *dharmakāya* are not produced by them;
rather, they are eternal dharmas that are manifested through them.
That which resembles [the cause] is called the seed.
Thus, the Liang translation of the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* states:
"The perfuming of hearing is merely the seed for the path of the four virtues."
The path of the four virtues can accomplish and manifest the four virtues.
These four virtues exist inherently from the beginning;
they do not arise from seeds.
Because it is designated by name according to its cause, it is called a "seed.

By this analogy, one should know that the mental states associated with the four wisdoms take that [nature] as their object; while appearing as if they were produced from it, they resemble the teaching of True Suchness (tathatā).
It is called the "seed.

If one were to concede that True Suchness (tathatā) is actually the seed capable of producing conditioned phenomena (saṃskṛta), it would contradict the first of the seven characteristics of seeds in the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*: that impermanent dharmas serve as causes.
This also contradicts the *Buddhadhātu-śāstra*, which states among the three natures that "one [nature] has a substantial entity capable of producing a substantial entity.

Question: If those of the two vehicles who possess a fixed nature do not become Buddhas, this would contradict the thirty-sixth fascicle of the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*, which says that stream-enterers (*srotāpanna*), once-returners (*sakṛdāgāmin*), non-returners (*anāgāmin*), arhats, and pratyekabuddhas shall all eventually attain Buddhahood.
Having heard this teaching, they do not give rise to faith;
it continues until it says, "This is called 'perpetually submerged.
The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* states:
"Whether they be śrāvakas or bodhisattvas, upon hearing the Dharma taught by me,
even as little as a single verse,
they will all undoubtedly attain Buddhahood," and so forth.
Answer: This teaching states that śrāvakas of indeterminate nature, those who have attained the four fruits, and pratyekabuddhas shall all attain Buddhahood;
it says that those who hear this and do not believe are called "perpetually submerged," and so forth.
It does not mean that all beings—whether of determinate or indeterminate nature—will necessarily attain Buddhahood.
Not so. How can Nirvana itself say,
"All shall become Buddhas"?
You do not understand my intention.
Furthermore, regarding the *Bodhicaryāvatāra-śāstra* and other such texts,
have you not seen the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, which states that one does not become a Buddha?
Question: Regarding those icchantikas who are certain not to attain Buddhahood, why does the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, in its thirty-sixth fascicle, state:
"If a person’s mind and speech are of discordant character and they speak with divergent words, saying that an icchantika cannot attain bodhi"?
Such a person also slanders the Buddha, the Dharma,
and the Saṅgha. According to the meaning of this passage,
if one were to say that an icchantika definitely cannot attain bodhi, [they would be slandering].
This is termed slandering the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha;
it does not preclude those who have entered only slightly.
If that were so, it would further contradict the statement in the *Ratnagotravibhāga*.
As for what was said previously— that icchantikas never enter nirvana and lack the nature of nirvana—
this was intended to turn back those who slander the Mahāyāna and those whose minds do not seek the Mahāyāna.
It is stated thus on account of immeasurable time,
because that pure nature truly exists.
The *Foxing lun* (Treatise on Buddha-nature) states:
"To speak of 'having nature' is an explicit teaching."
To speak of "the absence of intrinsic nature" is an incomplete teaching;
this continues up until the point where it is considered redundant.
Because the Buddha perceives that all sentient beings possess an intrinsically pure nature (*prakṛti-viśuddhi*),
they will certainly attain the pure *dharmakāya* at a later time;
it is by this principle that we know [this to be so].
There are no icchantikas who lack the buddha-nature,
nor are there any sentient beings who will not attain buddhahood.
This answer is based on the intention that the fundamental nature (dharmatā) is equal for all.
Furthermore, among those who are eternally submerged according to the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*,
the second type— though not an icchantika— is also termed "eternally submerged.
This refers to those among the three types of those lacking the dharma of nirvāṇa mentioned in the *Anuttarāśraya-sūtra* and other texts.
The second person says:
"The fifth chapter of the *Laṅkāvatāra* states that those of the vehicle of no-nature (*abhāva-yāna*) are likewise included in this assembly;
those who do not understand the teaching of *amala-vijñāna* are called 'perpetually submerged'."
There are seven types, each one distinct, as well as those for whom there is no nirvāṇa-dharma according to the first chapter of the *Anuttarāśrayasūtra*.
Question: If this is so, why do both the *Ratnagotravibhāga* and the *Buddhadhātu-śāstra* cite scriptural passages [to the contrary]?
The icchantika who falls into the category of those fixed in error has two kinds of bodies:
first, the fundamental dharma-body;
second, the body that accords with their will.
The sun of the Buddha’s wisdom illuminates these two bodies.
As for the "Dharma" of the Dharma-body,
it is the principle of *tathatā* (suchness).
As for the body that acts according to one's will,
it arises from the Buddha’s radiance in accordance with reality,
out of compassion for those who lack faith (icchantikas).
Regarding the two bodies of the icchantika:
first, it is for the sake of causing the dharma-body to arise;
second, it is for the sake of enabling the prolonged cultivation of bodhisattva practices through applied effort.
[Question: Is it established through contemplation?
[Answer: This is stated with reference to those icchantikas who possess the seed-nature (gotra);
it is not otherwise.
This contradicts the previous matter.
The *Nengpin* (Chapter on Capabilities) states:
"Sentient beings of the indeterminate group (*aniyata-rāśi*) give rise to these two matters as their function."
It does not state that the "determined class" (niyata-rāśi) serves as the function.
Furthermore, it says:
"This person, by virtue of the purified factors (viśuddha-aṅga), takes the purified nature (viśuddha-svabhāva) as the condition and as the cause."
The accomplishment of this contemplation does not occur without causes and conditions;
it cannot be accomplished through contemplation if it does not rely on these two factors.
There is no cause or condition;
one should cultivate this contemplation that those such as icchantikas lack the nature for nirvana.
Since icchantikas lack this contemplation,
we know that one must certainly rely on the contemplation of causes and conditions before the absence of intrinsic nature can be manifested.
Since contemplation is not permitted,
it is clearly understood that those lacking intrinsic nature cannot attain Buddhahood.
Furthermore, this is also consistent with what is said in the ninth fascicle of the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*:
That the light of the Great Nirvāṇa enters the pores of all sentient beings and is able to act as the cause for bodhi—
this meaning is not so.
Why is this? Because the World-Honored One has committed the four grave prohibitions,
acted as one who commits the five heinous crimes, and is an icchantika.
Regarding those for whom the light enters the body and acts as the cause for bodhi,
such individuals differ from those who purely maintain the precepts and cultivate various wholesome dharmas;
thus it was said by the Buddha.
Good son, with the exception of the icchantikas, all other sentient beings,
having heard this sutra,
will all be able to create the causes and conditions for bodhi.
One into whose pores the light of the sound of the Dharma enters will certainly attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi;
it is by this standard that one knows this.
As stated in the *Buddhatva-śāstra* and other cited sūtras,
those whose bodies are illuminated by the light of the Buddha’s solar wisdom so that they may grow toward awakening are people who possess the buddha-nature (*gotra*).
The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states that those who exclude the icchantikas are persons lacking the spiritual nature (*agotra*). This is not so.
Why is it that some are removed while others are not?
Furthermore, it says:
"If one is able to hear this Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra..."
Even those who have committed the four grave prohibitions or the five acts of immediate retribution can still create the causal conditions for bodhi;
the icchantikas, however, are not like this.
Although they may hear and receive this sublime sūtra,
they are unable to give rise to the causes for the path to bodhi;
furthermore, it contains many parables.
It is like withered wood or stone upon which water does not abide;
it is like a scorched seed that, even when encountering sweet rain, will never sprout.
Furthermore, it is said:
Even if all immeasurable sentient beings were to simultaneously achieve unexcelled bodhi,
these Tathāgatas would still not see those icchantikas attaining bodhi.
This is the explicit teaching on *nirvāṇa*.
How could one not believe that there are those who do not attain Buddhahood?
Thus we know that the sūtras speak of those called *icchantikas* as being "without nature" (*abhāva*).
Furthermore, it is said that one shall attain Buddhahood; this is stated with intentional ambiguity (*saṃdhyābhāṣita*),
based on the existence of the seeds [of enlightenment] while asserting their non-existence [in terms of a permanent self].
The various distinctions among the vehicles, their increases and decreases,
and their differences are explained in detail elsewhere; here,
I shall provide a brief outline of the general principles.
Other difficult points may be inferred accordingly.

This *Madhyāntavibhāga-prajñā-sūrya-śāstra* (Treatise on the Sun of Wisdom Distinguishing the Middle and the Extremes), Volume Four, was completed in the twelfth month of the twelfth year of the Hōreki era at a lodging in the city of Heian.
Copied from the manuscript held in the sutra repository of Zentō-ji Temple in Tado District, Sanuki Province;
upon its completion, it is dedicated to the four debts of gratitude and the ocean of the Dharma-realm, and dedicated toward unexcelled, great Bodhi.
In the tenth month of the year Kishi (1773), the second year of the An’ei era,
the śramaṇa Kiben of the Hossō school at the Sai-shitsu of Tōdai-ji [recorded this] at Jimon-in in Kōfuku-ji.
This was collated by combining the Chūnichi-sha original with the Tanki-ya edition.
Once the omissions were supplemented and the scribal errors corrected, the original characters were annotated in the margins for each character; these are the ones indicated there.
The late scholar Hōsō, Daikyō, of the Daitō-bō,
at the age of fifty-six,
recorded this based on the Imperial manuscript preserved at the Hontan-gi-ya.
On the twelfth day of the twelfth month of the second year of the Jōgen era, in the year of Wuchen (1208),
at the hour of Shen, in the southern wing of the Hōtō-in at Higashitani in Saigoku.
I transcribe this. By the power of this transcription,
may I be reborn in the Heaven of the Universal Rulers (Īśāna).
Hearing the Dharma leads to awakening and understanding;
one will certainly realize non-retrogression.
On the eighteenth day of the twelfth month of that year, he passed away.
Written by Eikyū Gakuban during the middle of the fifth month in the eighth year of the Kyōhō era.
Copied from the original manuscript and proofread once.
Shūshin.
